scope: All 35 variable definitions, all 78 original links, two added definitional links, and all 10 highlighted loop paths reviewed for semantics and structure. Review-level evidence was checked at the cited passages; underlying primary studies were not independently reappraised.
judgment: The original highlighted cycles close and have correct sign parity. This does not establish the validity of all variable constructs, causal directions or complete feedback mechanisms.
limits: This review is not independent human expert approval or a systematic reassessment of all underlying studies.
New operational definitions are proposed research-design choices requiring stakeholder agreement and measurement validation.
No empirical effect sizes, relative strengths, simulated trajectories or dominant loops are claimed.

findings.issue: Mixed units in household resources and housing prices
findings.action: Separate disposable income, monthly market rents and actual payment burden; rental-tenure restrictions are explicit.

findings.issue: Physical activity was broader than traffic exposure
findings.action: Use active-travel time and active-travel injury incidence; distinguish per-resident incidence from hazard per unit exposure.

findings.issue: Some direct arrows lacked a distinct or well-supported mechanism
findings.action: Retire generic voice-to-protection, the unspecified displacement shortcut and the unsupported mental-health-to-work direction.

findings.issue: A vector of needs gaps has no single signed direction
findings.action: Propose an any-unmet-need prevalence gap with explicit thresholds and overlap conditions; preserve domain-specific reporting.

findings.issue: Health disparity and normative inequity were conflated
findings.action: Specify poor-self-rated-health prevalence gap; mark morbidity-to-self-rating as a hypothesis and fairness as a separate judgment.

findings.issue: Population and attribute mappings were easy to overread
findings.action: Flag priority-to-neighborhood voice/traffic mappings, cooling attributes and sector allocation conditions.

findings.issue: A source locator understated the available productivity discussion
findings.action: Point A34 to S6 Section 6.4 pp.22–23; distinguish productivity costs from employment and household-income feedback.

findings.issue: All highlighted loops could appear equally established
findings.action: Show evidence categories and review notes on loop cards and detail panels; policy and exploratory loops remain hypotheses.

variables.reason: An unordered vector of five needs gaps has no single increase or decrease. Propose one explicit scalar while retaining domain-specific reporting.

measurementNote.after: 100 × [P(at least one unmet need | priority) − P(at least one unmet need | reference)]. Thresholds and membership fixed; no domain weights.

definition.before: Excess unmet built-environment needs among priority groups relative to a locally defined, better-served reference group. Higher means less equity. A conceptual set of domain-specific gaps, with no invented weighting or scalar score.
definition.after: Percentage-point difference between priority and reference groups in the share of residents with at least one prespecified unmet built-environment need. Use locally agreed, group-appropriate thresholds for the five stated domains. This proposed non-compensatory indicator is not a validated scale; report each domain alongside it. A positive gap indicates priority-group disadvantage.

variables.reason: Separate a measurable health disparity from a normative judgment of inequity; choose one outcome rather than an undefined physical/mental composite.

measurementNote.after: 100 × [P(poor self-rated health | priority) − P(poor self-rated health | reference)]. Prespecify response categories and any age standardization.

definition.before: Unfair, avoidable excess physical and mental ill health among priority groups relative to the local reference group; health inequality requires normative assessment to call it inequity.
definition.after: Percentage-point difference between priority and reference groups in the prevalence of poor self-rated health, using the same prespecified survey definition and period. A positive gap indicates priority-group disadvantage. Interpreting it as inequity additionally requires an assessment of unfairness and avoidability; physical or mental morbidity does not mechanically determine self-rating.
